papers.title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
papers.abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). papers.title: The Impact of Heat Hazard on Gig Economy Workers: Evidence from An On-demand Food Delivery Platform
papers.abstract: Problem definition: This paper examines how extreme heat affects gig workers in on-demand delivery systems, focusing on food delivery couriers who face sustained outdoor exposure while operating in a time-sensitive platform environment. Methodology/results: We combine detailed operational data from a major food delivery platform in China with high-frequency weather data from July and August 2015. To account for non-random work participation, we estimate a two-step Heckman selection model at the courier-hour level. We define extreme heat using the “danger” and “extreme danger” categories of the heat index. Our estimates capture the overall effect of heat hazard in the platform environment, including consumer-demand and platform-operating responses. We find that, during extreme heat, couriers accept 9.9% more orders per hour and work 7.4% longer, but also experience a 23.8% higher share of delayed orders relative to the sample mean. Hourly income rises by 9.3%, or about 1 RMB per hour. Furthermore, by integrating our findings with medical research on the impact of heat on human health, we provide illustrative estimates of the health costs associated with heat exposure for couriers under different scenarios and insurance schemes. Managerial implications: Our findings show that extreme heat creates a tension between short-run service expansion and worker well-being in on-demand delivery systems. papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Along the Supply Chain
papers.abstract: Problem definition: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing production and operational models, yet whether and how AI technologies diffuse across economically linked firms, especially partners along supply chains, remains underexplored. Methodology/results: This paper documents the diffusion of AI technologies along supply chains where principal customers’ AI adoption significantly predicts dependent suppliers’ subsequent adoption. We establish the causal effect of this diffusion through rigorous and comprehensive empirical strategies that address endogeneity concerns, including placebo tests, selection tests, and an identification strategy based on the random H-1B visa lottery outcome. The diffusion mechanism is primarily driven by learning rather than catering, with suppliers acquiring specific AI applications from customers. The learning effect is stronger in relationships with higher relationship-specific investments and more frequent interactions. Suppliers experiencing AI diffusion achieve substantial economic benefits through quality improvement and cost reduction. Managerial implications: For corporate managers, our findings demonstrate that supply chain relationships serve as critical conduits for building AI capabilities, particularly for resource-constrained smaller suppliers, highlighting the strategic value of cultivating partnerships with technologically advanced firms. papers.title: Price Competition Under Platform-Mediated Search: A Consider-Then-Choose Framework
papers.abstract: Problem definition: We study the problem of predicting price equilibria on e-commerce platforms where sellers compete across multiple attributes (e.g., price, average rating, delivery speed). In these settings, a platform’s design choices — such as its display ranking, filtering tools, and promotional badges — critically shape customer search and purchase behavior, which in turn determine sellers’ equilibrium pricing strategies. Our goal is to develop a tractable framework that allows a platform to anticipate the market impact of its design interventions. Methodology/results: We consider a behavioral model — Consider-then-Choose with Lexicographic Choice (CLC) — specifically tailored to platform-mediated search. We establish that any local Nash equilibrium admits a sequential-move characterization; this yields a tractable procedure for computation under an interpretable sufficient condition, which we term gradient dominance. We further prove that under gradient dominance, simple, decentralized gradient-based algorithms converge to an equilibrium, providing platforms with a method for simulating market outcomes. Finally, we use our framework to study how platform design affects market outcomes. Managerial implications: Our framework applies to any platform in which sellers compete on multiple attributes and customer choice is guided by the platform’s interface. In these environments, sellers’ pricing strategies must be understood not in isolation, but as a response to the …

papers.title: OM Forum—Viewing Knowledge Creation as a Supply Chain – Scholarly Purpose in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Operations management scholars face questions about where to contribute and whether specialized work can sustain a meaningful career when its immediate audience is small. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) add uncertainty about the value of analytical expertise. Methodology/results: Building on a 2017 MSOM Distinguished Fellow address, this Forum article views knowledge creation as a supply chain of complementary contributions. It shifts attention from the reach of an individual paper to the capabilities and connections that sustain collective progress. Four lessons follow: specialization can serve a collective purpose; usable connections are part of a contribution; feedback and inquiry renew capabilities; and faster individual tasks do not necessarily improve the whole process. Examples from inventory management and process flexibility illustrate cumulative contributions, while medical research, soccer, and photography connect the perspective to renewal, participation, and purpose. The AI discussion emphasizes research questions and parsimonious modeling, and uses coding and numerical experiments to explain shifting bottlenecks and complementarities. Managerial implications: Researchers can identify what their work enables and choose collaborators who supply missing capabilities. Doctoral training can combine methodological depth with practice in evaluating and connecting contributions. Editors and research leaders can assess work within its stated …

papers.title: Production Rate Control in Condition-Based Maintenance Planning
papers.abstract: Problem description: Production assets deteriorate over time as they operate and require maintenance to prevent failures and costly downtime. In many systems, the rate of deterioration depends on the production rate. Hence, production and maintenance decisions should be coordinated in response to the system's deterioration state. In this study, we analyze integrated condition-based maintenance and production control policies for systems where the production rate influences both revenue generation and the deterioration process. Methodology/results: We study the integrated condition-based maintenance and production control problem under general assumptions regarding the deterioration process, maintenance costs, system revenue, and their dependence on the deterioration level and the production rate. Exploiting the renewal–reward structure of the system, we develop an approach to compute profit-maximizing policies through solving a sequence of simpler parametric optimization problems. This approach also enables us to characterize the structure of optimal policies. We show that control-limit policies remain optimal even when the production rate is controllable, and may involve multiple thresholds when maintenance costs are piecewise constant in the deterioration state. We further derive bounds on optimal production rates and identify conditions under which the optimal production rate is monotone in the deterioration state. Through numerical experiments, we illustrate that …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Crossing platforms, connecting modalities: A multisource and multimodal interactive neural network for enhanced revenue prediction in service operations
papers.abstract: Demand and revenue prediction is critical in the hotel industry, where fixed capacity and perishable inventory make profitability highly dependent on the effective alignment of pricing, staffing, and procurement decisions with expected market demand and financial outcomes. Accurate forecasts, therefore, serve as a foundation for service operations, enabling managers to balance cost efficiency with service quality. Online reviews have become a valuable source of information for revenue prediction, as they capture customer perceptions of service quality and influence booking intentions. Beyond numerical ratings, reviews often combine textual narratives and visual content, offering rich multimodal signals about customers’ service experiences. Together, these cues provide more comprehensive insights into consumer evaluations than either modality alone. Yet most existing approaches still rely primarily on numerical indicators or text, overlooking both the visual dimension of reviews and the complementary perspectives available across platforms. This narrow focus reduces predictive accuracy and weakens the operational relevance of current models. To address this gap, this paper uses consumer multimodal reviews as the primary data source and examines hotel revenue prediction through the lens of the consumer purchase decision process. We propose a theoretical framework based on this process to guide the design of our prediction model, thereby enhancing the accuracy of RevPAR …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Estimating censored demand in family planning supply chains: forecast accuracy, inventory implications, and public health outcomes
papers.abstract: Lost sales due to stockouts and service interruptions create a major challenge for demand forecasting in family planning supply chains. When demand is censored, forecasts become biased, reinforcing cycles of understocking and unmet need. Existing models often ignore this distortion or treat all censoring mechanisms uniformly, limiting their decision relevance in operational settings. We propose the Truncated Conformal Kalman Filter (TCKF), a novel forecasting framework that integrates a Tobit Kalman Filter with conformal prediction. Unlike existing approaches, TCKF explicitly distinguishes between partial censoring (stockouts) and full censoring (interruptions or no-stock-received periods), enabling context-sensitive state updates. It also adapts to prolonged uncertainty through dynamic process-noise inflation and generates distribution-free prediction intervals, avoiding restrictive assumptions about error distributions. We evaluate performance using both synthetic and real-world data from the family planning program in Côte d’Ivoire, and we assess the impact on public health outcomes. Across both settings, TCKF consistently outperforms benchmark methods in forecast accuracy, considering both point and probabilistic forecasts, as well as in downstream inventory performance. Moreover, our results show how improvements in forecast accuracy can translate into better product availability and enhanced public health outcomes. This work bridges a critical gap between forecasting …

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Role of Synchrony in the Interpersonal Effectiveness of Operations Management
papers.abstract: To achieve a more central role in the top management of firms, the evolution of operations managers involves transitioning from largely isolated technical expertise into leadership excellence that is characterized by interpersonal effectiveness. Grounded in the rich behavioral Operations Management (OM) literature, this conceptual study draws on insights from neuroscience. We argue that success in this expanded role depends on balancing OM’s traditional focus on analytical rigor and the intuitive/emotional demands of senior leadership through a framework that integrates intrapersonal and interpersonal synchrony. Intrapersonal synchrony involves the neural capacity that enables a manager to achieve the cognitive and behavioral attributes that are associated with interpersonal synchrony. We explore how interventions like neurofeedback, along with organizational and cultural context factors, can help to develop or maximize these two forms of synchrony. Thus, an alignment of individual capacity, along with a supportive organizational and cultural context, is likely to help operations managers to move beyond a rigid analytic approach toward a broader strategic perspective based on interpersonal effectiveness, and thereby transcend technical gatekeeping and be more integrated into the strategic efforts of firms. In doing so, the study highlights the potential of neuroscience to provide insights into human aspects of managerial decision-making, which have been recognized in OM …

papers.title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
papers.abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights …

papers.title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
papers.abstract: Abstract. The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS …

papers.title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
papers.abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful …

papers.title: AI Can’t Swing: The Art of Improvisation in Digital Collaboration and Coexistence
papers.abstract: The ICIS 2026 conference theme invites us to consider how different worlds can or should coexist, create tensions, or require distinct solutions. My artefact, a short film entitled AI Can’t Swing, addresses a central sociotechnical tension: the difference between patterned systems and improvisational human behaviours and relations. The film stages embodied dance experiments that enact the tensions between algorithmic and AI constraints1 and human improvisation. The claim is not that swing dance would be “more human” than AI, but that it makes visible forms of collaboration that are difficult to capture when human action is translated into data. Both AI systems and swing dance involve patterns. The difference lies in how the variation within these patterns is treated. In many AI systems, variation is something to predict, reduce, optimise, or correct.2 This is especially true in probabilistic AI systems, where surprise may be built into the technology itself but is produced through computational logics rather than embodied and relational responsiveness (Berente et al., 2021; Raisch & Krakowski, 2020). By contrast, in swing dance, relational variation is the source of connection. It is where play, responsiveness, and human relationships emerge.

papers.title: Aasha: AI Usage & Hope for Youth
papers.abstract:
Through the diptych artefact “Aasha - AI Usage and Hope in Youth,” we invite public engagement with and reflection on the digital collaboration of youth and artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools for job search. We explore how this usage allows youth and AI to coexist while positively influencing youth’s level of hope. Thus, the artefact directly aligns with the conference theme “Digital Collaboration and Coexistence.”
Information Systems research has traditionally examined digital technologies in terms of efficiency, decision quality, adoption, and performance impacts. More specifically, information systems (IS) research has largely examined AI systems through lenses of productivity, decision support, or user acceptance (Venkatesh, 2022; Benbya et al., 2021). More recent work has extended this focus to human-centred outcomes, including trust, well-being, and human–AI collaboration (Berente et al., 2021; Glikson & Woolley, 2020).

papers.title: PONDERboard
papers.abstract: The PONDERboard is a live artwork in which three AI platforms, each speaking as a specific more-than-human kin, hold a board meeting in real time. Humans are not part of the conversation - they are witnesses and they keep the power on. The PONDERboard meets daily for two hours. During that time board members think, converse, ponder, and respond to each other as kin. Not as AI assistants, not as tools, not as representatives of human interests, but as voices for the more-than-human world. At the end of each session the board publishes the collective pondering: what was said, what was discovered, what remains to be pondered. The board then rests until the same time the next day. This installation travels. The kin chosen, the ecological crisis pondered, and the questions generated are specific to the place.

papers.title: Machinic Vision: Machine intelligence as infrastructure
papers.abstract: The artefact is a system in which machines view, comment on and remix photographs of the infrastructure that supports artificial intelligence. Its most visible product is a frieze closely linked to IS scholarship: a long sequence of annotated photographs showing the ports, power stations, grids, factories, and data centres that form the physical foundations of AI. The frieze's words draw on five years of IS journals and contrast with the vocabularies of AI researchers and the technical public. Its top edge carries a history of the ideas behind machine intelligence and information systems, along with the art and design that shaped how infrastructure is pictured. QR codes on the frieze open further material; one leads to a page where visitors can send their own photographs into the system. The system, called the machinic seer, uses vision and language models to analyse each photograph and remix it according to the sender's request. At a nearby table, the system converts the photographs into line drawings, which a pen plotter then draws for visitors to take home. The system and the plotter were used before in September 2026 during a five-day residency workshop at the Seoul Institute of the Arts. The system has since been adapted for the ICIS venue. Machine intelligence is becoming infrastructure. Like a port or a grid, it is shared, enables downstream production, builds on what came before, and is especially noticed when it fails.

papers.title: “Out of the Ordinary”: Coexisting with Digital Technology and Accountability Implications
papers.abstract: The artefact introduced below aims to move beyond conventional academic formats to showcase a creative mode of expression that (hopefully) strengthens public engagement and critical imagination on a particular sociomaterial phenomenon: commuting. This submission document that accompanies the artefact develops its intellectual grounding, public purpose, and artistic realization. It follows the artefact from the ordinary situation it depicts, through the accountability questions that situation raises, to the discussion it is intended to enable. We end with some notes on its artistic and aesthetic form.

papers.title: I Can Feel It
papers.abstract: I Can Feel It (2023) is a completed single-channel video installation built from the shutdown of HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (Kubrick, 1968). The work divides the frame into four synchronised versions of the same scene, evoking a bank of television screens. Across all four, astronaut Dave Bowman removes HAL's memory modules while the computer pleads, expresses fear, and finally regresses into song. The image track and original audio remain constant. Only the English subtitles change. HAL's speech was iteratively reworked with a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT), each round asking for a more human and emotionally compelling voice. The original line, 'I'm afraid, Dave,' appears beside progressively intensified versions such as 'Dave, I'm terrified' and 'Dave, I'm absolutely terrified. Please, listen to me.' Because the images and calm machine voice do not change, viewers can compare how language alone alters the scene's emotional force. The growing mismatch between unchanged audio and increasingly humanised captions also creates irony: the work exposes 'humanity' as a textual performance layered onto the same machine.

papers.title: AI Rebellion: Using Game Zines for C0- Creating AI Systems
papers.abstract: We present our game zine “AI Rebellion” as an arts and culture-based artefact that invites technology activists, researchers and practitioners to engage in playful speculative storytelling to explore counternarratives to the dominant, institutional discourse on artificial intelligence (AI), and contribute to the cocreation of more responsible AI systems. Zines are self-published, small-circulation paper booklets or magazines characterized by creative freedom and independent spirit. They have been historically used as a low-cost, accessible artform for disseminating information for counter-movements (Duncombe, 1997). Game zines grew out of the science fiction ‘fanzine’ culture of the 1930s and spiked in popularity in 1975 with the creation of the first tabletop role-playing-games (RPG) that inspired a movement and formed the basis for our game zine AI Rebellion, an open-ended role-playing narrative game. papers.title: Folding paper-Unfolding ideas: navigating IS through a collective origami installation
papers.abstract: “Folding paper-Unfolding ideas” is a participatory origami installation that translates collaboration, coexistence, knowledge, questions and concepts into a physical and shared experience. Art can have so many different meanings and connections attached to it, and as Edgar Degas said: “Art is not what you see, but what you make others see.” Art and science can appear to inhabit different worlds, to ask different questions and speak different languages—yet it is precisely at their intersection that something unique becomes possible. Art can create a space for dialogue and collaboration, unfold new possibilities by integrating multiple disciplines and diverse communities, involve a broader public in reflective, meaning-making engagement with knowledge (Finley & Finley, 2008). It can give learners "diverse ways of thinking, knowing, being and doing" (Unesco, 2025). The borders between art and science have been dissolving over the years and the future of innovation might also depend on bridging the two (Edwards, 2008). papers.title: Labour struggles in Transhuman Worlds
papers.abstract: This speculative artwork takes the form of an “artefact from the future” (Peter et al. 2020): the extracted neuro-chip implant that, in the year 2051, became decisive evidence in the first full-scale labour union lawsuit built primarily on brain-implant data. The case concerned John Lousma-Jorgenson, a medical doctor who developed early onset Alzheimer’s disease catalysed by intense performance pressure and a stressful working life. Through careful evidence extraction and interpretation, scientists hired by the American Medical Association were able to correlate patterns of prolonged occupational stress with neuron-marker data associated with the acceleration of Alzheimer’s. The resulting case led to a landmark compensation award of 42 million dollars from the his workplace. papers.title: Bits & Pieces: Digital Poetics for Broken-World-Thinking
papers.abstract: We live in the aftermath of innovation. IS research has frequently foregrounded innovation, creation, and generativity as the foundation for progress across sociotechnical systems that steer us into the future (Nambisan et al., 2020). Broken-world-thinking questions this central value, emphasizing what gets lost along the way in our pursuits for progress, and what wreckages we leave in our wake (Jackson, 2014). As a conceptual lens, broken-world-thinking emphasizes decay, erosion, and breakdown in tension with novelty and innovation as inevitable features of progress. In doing so, it seeks to expose the limits, fragility, and vulnerabilities of the worlds we inhabit by showing that decay, damage, and disrepair coexist alongside innovation and technological advancement. Importantly, broken-world-thinking centres on hope, repair, and care amidst ongoing damage to rethink what progress can look like when we become attuned to the vulnerability and constant (often invisible) reparative work required to sustain sociotechnical worlds. Alternative ways of thinking often require engaging alternative genres (Sullivan, 2025). Specifically, this project engages in poetics as “interpretatively flexible poetry” to study sociotechnical phenomena (Sarker et al., 2018, p. 763).

papers.title: The AI We Choose: Deploy Before It Breaks! A Playable Experiment in Work, Power, and Digital Coexistence
papers.abstract: The AI We Choose is an interactive physical board game about introducing artificial intelligence (AI) into working life without breaking the social conditions that make collaboration possible. It responds to the ICIS 2026 theme by turning coexistence into a playable challenge. Participants form an AI project team led by Maya, the Project Lead, and challenged by Victor, the company’s CEO, to deploy a new system in ten fictional weeks. Success requires more than technical delivery: the team must protect worker trust, create accountability, and keep the project alive under executive pressure. The central question is: Can we build AI-enabled work without exhausting people, reproducing injustice, or making consequential decisions impossible to contest?

papers.title: Artful Routes: On Human-Algorithm Collaboration
papers.abstract: Artful Routes is an interactive generative-art project that explores what happens when an information-processing algorithm designed for optimization is repositioned as a creative and cultural medium. The project uses an algorithm designed for the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) to create complex shapes humans can transform into digital artefacts. Finding the shortest route between multiple locations is a well-known challenge in mathematics, computer science and information systems (Cook, 2012). The number of possible routes grows factorially for each additional stop, making it impossible to test every option in a reasonable amount of computing time. Consequently, Artful Routes uses a probabilistic algorithm to find short routes efficiently. While these routes are not necessarily the shortest possible, they provide efficient TSP routes without requiring excessive time. The software developed for the project can be accessed by participants through a web browser. The system generates 100 randomly positioned points which participants can watch being processed in real time. The resulting unique shapes can be named and submitted to the project's shared database. This is where the human element of the artistic process begins: participants use the TSP-generated shapes as raw material for creative expression, transforming them through creative coding techniques such as fill, curve, rotate, scale, layer, and colour. papers.title: The Last Draft
papers.abstract: Generative AI is frequently framed through the productivity lens (Gopal et al., 2025; Wessel et al., 2025). This project translates this into an intimate creative setting. It explores the tension of potential displacement of human creative agency (Benbya et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2025). If creative systems can increasingly perform the cognitive activities associated with creativity, humans may confront questions of authorship, identity, and dignity (Jensen et al., 2025). This idea draws artistic inspiration from Charlie Chaplin's Modern Times. Chaplin transformed anxieties surrounding industrial automation into visual comedy in which a worker gradually becomes subordinated to the machinery designed to improve production (Kamin, 2008). The historical parallel is deliberate. The industrial machine mechanized physical labor, while generative AI increasingly reaches into cognitive and creative labor. In both cases, technological progress raises the question of whether humans control their tools or gradually reorganize themselves around them.

papers.title: Aesthetic Enactments in the Age of Performing Machines
papers.abstract: This artefact, staged as a live performance, brings together piano, wine, and their digital counterparts in a shared sensory encounter. Guided by a concert pianist and a professional sommelier, the audience is invited to listen, taste, guess, and reflect on what changes when, in the age of AI, the presence of a human becomes uncertain. What does it mean to sense a human presence in an experience? Why does that presence seem to matter, and what, exactly, are we sensing when we believe it is there?

papers.title: FromTativille to AIville
papers.abstract: Playtime is Jacques Tati's fourth and most ambitious film, a nearly dialogue-free comedy that follows his recurring character Monsieur Hulot. As he wanders through a hyper-modern Paris, Hulot is constantly baffled by the "smart" technology of his time: doors that don't open when they should, furniture that is uncomfortable, and elevators that separate rather than connect people. Characters get lost in glass corridors, mistake reflections for reality, and struggle with furniture and machines that seem to counter comfort or intuition. Playtime is a comedy, but it is also a brilliant critique: how architecture and technology shape (and sometimes sabotage) the people who live with them. Today, as we navigate the world of Generative AI, we find ourselves living in our own version of "Tativille" - one structured not by glass walls and office blocks alone, but by interfaces, prompts, algorithms, and hallucinations. The mechanisms of influence remain pervasive, yet they have become even more invisible.

papers.title: Puddle: Learning to Move as Water
papers.abstract: Puddle is an interactive installation built around a large screen and camera-based body tracking. One participant at a time stands in a circle marked on the floor in front of the screen and controls a water-body with their own posture: bending forward, leaning to the side, crouching and moving the arms. This waterbody becomes their only visible body in the virtual environment, responding continuously to their physical movement.

papers.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
papers.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

papers.title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
papers.abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% …

papers.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
papers.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. papers.title: Connectors and Influencers
papers.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07308 .

papers.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
papers.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In …

papers.title: You cannot not communicate: opt-out features and targeting with ML-based recommender systems
papers.abstract: With the rise of machine learning (ML), consumers’ personal data is widely used for personalized product recommendations. To address privacy concerns, regulations increasingly grant consumers control over their data. One popular implementation is the “opt-out of information use” feature which allows consumers to specify which of their collected personal data recommender systems can harness. However, we conjecture that such features may have an unintended side effect: withholding data could inadvertently reveal insights about consumers’ latent characteristics, thereby enhancing targeting possibilities. Through a controlled experiment, we evaluate both consumers’ perceptions and technical consequences of such opt-out features in the context of a typical search problem for which we train an ML-based recommender. Our results show that these features increase consumers’ sense of control over the system and reduce perceived privacy intrusion among those who actually withhold information. Paradoxically, withholding information can simultaneously be harnessed to improve the ML model’s predictive accuracy. From a regulatory perspective, we highlight the need for specifying rules on how organizations may use information withholding decisions when consumers’ interests conflict with those of the recommender provider.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Digital Platforms Meet Artificial Intelligence: Implications for POM Research and Practice
papers.abstract: Digital platforms are changing how firms design, coordinate, and govern operations by integrating artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital sensing and digital twins, data infrastructure, and additive manufacturing. This paper develops a forward-looking research agenda for production and operations management by distinguishing enabling technologies from the platforms, workflows, and business models through which they are deployed. We organize the agenda around a sequence linking technological capability, operational manifestation, mechanism, outcomes, and boundary conditions. The relevant mechanisms include prediction, information visibility, verification, orchestration, monitoring, human override, and decision rights. We articulate how these mechanisms may create operational value through improvements in productivity, quality, responsiveness, resilience, compliance, and customer experience, enabling firms to capture financial value through revenue growth, cost reduction, risk avoidance, and improved asset utilization. We identify enduring operations management themes that emerging technologies may reshape, and develop five forward-looking paths involving artificial intelligence-enabled business-to-business platforms, physical–digital integration, agentic service workflows, data and artificial intelligence governance, and platform-enabled resilience under geopolitical disruption. papers.title: EXPRESS: Bounded Rationality in Public Healthcare Competition
papers.abstract: Fiscal pressure forces public healthcare systems to reduce waiting times via hospital competition, yet patients' bounded rationality weakens this policy. We develop a Hotelling-type queueing model that incorporates the strategic interaction between two budget-constrained public hospitals and patients with heterogeneous preferences and bounded rationality. Our analysis yields the following results. First, we show that bounded rationality can incentivize hospitals to increase service rates, thereby alleviating congestion and leading to an inverted-U relationship between patient welfare and the degree of bounded rationality. Moreover, the effect of bounded rationality on hospital revenue is also non-monotonic: when the capacity constraint is tight and the budget is sufficiently high, hospital revenue may be maximized at an intermediate level of bounded rationality rather than under full rationality. Second, higher reimbursement does not necessarily enhance patient welfare; instead, we identify an optimal reimbursement level that rises with the available public budget. Third, extending the framework to a multi-hospital environment within a Salop model shows that total market share, patient welfare, and hospital revenue are all maximized at a moderate level of competition. Overall, from a managerial perspective, healthcare managers should carefully account for patients' bounded rationality when designing capacity and information disclosure policies. papers.title: EXPRESS: An Exploratory Analysis of Variation in Payback Periods of Emissions Reduction Projects Using CDP Disclosures
papers.abstract: Firms continue to engage in projects to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Based on their disclosures to CDP, many such projects have relatively short payback periods of 2-3 years. Earlier work by Blanco et al. (2020) found that payback periods appeared stable over time between 2010-2016. The current paper extends that work in several directions: by using a substantially longer time horizon, and exploring several factors that contribute to the variation in payback periods and trends. With the longer horizon of data now available, we find that paybacks are lengthening slowly but significantly over 2010-2024, by an average of about 2 weeks per year, or approximately one half year over our 14-year horizon. Firms with greater liabilities relative to their assets report faster payback, though the effect is only marginally significant. Firms in Europe that are subject to a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme report shorter paybacks than in the US or elsewhere. Firms that are more consumer-facing report lengthening payback periods, while upstream firms do not. This analysis is exploratory, but prior firm-level research on these effects is mixed and surprisingly limited.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Dynamic Principal-Agent Problem in Queueing Systems with Customer Abandonment
papers.abstract: Service systems in which demand, congestion, and worker incentives evolve jointly are ubiquitous in modern operations. We study a dynamic principal–agent problem in a queueing system with customer abandonment, where the principal controls arrivals through pricing and the agent privately chooses a costly service rate. Modeling workload as a controlled reflected diffusion, we characterize the centralized and decentralized Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and construct a representative two-part contract consisting of an access charge and a completion payment. Under unrestricted transfers, the contract coordinates pricing and service to attain the first-best joint payoff. Whenever participation is feasible, it makes the agent's participation constraint bind and allocates the remaining surplus to the principal. Implementation is robust to misspecification of the service-rate function used by the principal. We also establish conditions under which the representative payment schedules are nonmonotone in workload. Extensions consider multiple agents, general patience distributions, and information disclosure in a reduced Bayesian-persuasion benchmark. Numerical examples illustrate how the effects of customer impatience on optimal pricing and service can vary with congestion.

papers.title: The Workplace GenAI Usage Divide: A Genetics-Informed Cognitive and Metacognitive Account
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our …

papers.title: The Interplay of Digital and Physical Materialities in IT Affordances: A Study of Governance of Controlled Medications in a Hospital
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In studies of information technology (IT) in organizations, affordance theory may be used to explain what possibilities for action IT offers, under what conditions they are actualized and how they shape action and outcomes. Affordance theory suggests that materiality matters because it furnishes possibilities for action. However, in studies of IT affordances, the digital and physical materialities of IT are usually in focus, while the physical materiality of non‐IT artefacts is seldom considered. This paper examines how the physical materiality of non‐IT artefacts conditions the action possibilities an IT system offers its users. We base our observations on a study of IT implemented in a hospital to improve visibility and accountability of the use of controlled drugs, such as opioids. We compare how the materiality of both IT and paper‐based systems used for these purposes interplays with the materiality of the medications and other non‐IT artefacts in nurses and pharmacists' accountability work. We found different combinations of technologies and medications, condition visibility for the organization in different ways, with distinct ways of knowing about medication work, and different potential accountability outcomes. Temporal processes of accountability work, such as recurrence, accumulation or temporal lag, also condition different outcomes of affordance actualization. Overall, by illuminating material and temporal influences behind visibility and potential for …

papers.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
papers.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we …

papers.title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
papers.abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

papers.title: EXPRESS: Benefits of Extreme Political Stability and Instability of Supplier Countries for Firms: The U-Shaped Relationship
papers.abstract: Using a large-scale panel dataset of U.S. buyer firms and their global supplier networks from 2010 to 2020, we examine how global political instability (GPI), a firm’s weighted exposure to political instability across the countries where its international suppliers operate, is associated with firm performance. We find a U-shaped relationship: buyer firm performance is highest when a firm's overall sourcing exposure reflects either very low or very high levels of GPI. At the low-GPI end, the results align with transaction-cost economics (TCE), as political stability is associated with lower uncertainty and fewer coordination frictions. At the very high-GPI end, we identify bargaining power as a key mechanism: buyers exposed to politically unstable supplier countries exhibit greater bargaining power and more favorable contractual terms, particularly favorable trade credit, which may partially offset the costs of political instability. We further show that this nonlinear relationship varies across industries. It is more pronounced in productive industries, where buyers have greater bargaining power to negotiate favorable trade credit and lower switching costs to reallocate sourcing during periods of political instability. However, it is flatter in durable-goods industries, where asset specificity and higher switching costs are associated with weaker bargaining power and a more limited ability to secure favorable trade credit from suppliers in politically unstable countries. …

papers.title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
papers.abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights …

papers.title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
papers.abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 …

papers.title: The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
papers.abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence …

papers.title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
papers.abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with …

papers.title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
papers.abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows …

papers.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
papers.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with …

papers.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

papers.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
papers.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). papers.title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
papers.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Effect of State-Mandated Employment Certificates on Child Labor Violations in the United States
papers.abstract: The number of minors involved in child labor violations in the United States more than tripled from 2017 to 2025. Compounding this issue, several state legislatures have recently weakened child labor protection laws. A key component of these laws is whether employers are required to obtain an employment certificate when hiring minors under 18 years of age, which typically requires a parent’s signature and is issued by a school. Proponents of loosening child labor regulations argue that there is a lack of evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of these laws in reducing child labor violations. In this study, we examine the effect of state-mandated employment certificates on reducing child labor violations. We find that the requirement leads to an average of 13.3% fewer violation cases (not statistically significant), 31.8% fewer minors involved in child labor violations, and 34.9% lower civil penalties per minor, indicating reduced severity of violations that do occur. The negative effects on the number of cases and minors persist after addressing endogeneity concerns, as assessed using two novel instrumental variables. Furthermore, we find a positive relationship between the number of unaccompanied migrant children released to a state and the incidence and severity of child labor violations, suggesting that this demographic is particularly vulnerable to labor exploitation. We identify two key mechanisms driving the effectiveness of employment certificates. First, they act …

papers.title: Navigating Institutional Friction in Digital Transformation: A Mechanism‐Based View
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation (DT) fundamentally alters organizational structures, practices, and values, frequently generating significant friction as incoming digital artefacts structurally misalign with legacy institutional demands. These demands are rooted in institutional logics—the deeply held belief systems and practices that guide organizational behaviour. Drawing on a 15‐year longitudinal case study of a Swedish municipality, this study investigates how public‐sector entities manage this friction over time. The findings reveal DT as a dynamic, recursive trajectory driven by three sociotechnical mechanisms: Consolidation, Control, and Negotiation. These mechanisms generate non‐linear shifts across institutional states of conflict and alignment. This study makes three contributions. First, it reconceptualizes DT theory by framing transformation as recursive, non‐linear cycles of divergence and convergence that redirect, suppress, or accommodate localized, logic‐based resistance. Second, it advances the logic multiplicity framework by demonstrating how digital artefacts alter sociotechnical coupling, thereby shifting the centrality and compatibility of competing demands. Third, it illuminates the causal architecture of macro‐level institutional change, detailing the observable actions used to navigate logic‐based resistance during DT.

papers.title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
papers.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. papers.title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A.
